 A Bipartisan Senate Bill Could Change How the IRS Deals With Taxpayers
 Jordan Major 2026년 10월 29일 목 오전 11:05 UTC 0 
Waiting weeks for a tax refund, spending hours trying to reach the IRS, or
struggling to resolve a mistake on your tax return might be frustrating,
especially when you're trying to check up on your
financial health . Now, lawmakers from both parties want to make those
experiences easier for Americans.
The bipartisan Taxpayer Assistance and Service Act (TAS) could change how
millions of taxpayers interact with the IRS, from tracking refunds to getting
help with tax problems. The legislation has already passed the Senate
unanimously and includes dozens of reforms designed to make the agency more
responsive while strengthening protections for taxpayers.

 Republicans and Democrats back major IRS changes
On September 30, the Senate unanimously approved the Taxpayer Assistance and
Service Act, a package of 65 reforms aimed at improving IRS services and
taxpayer rights. The legislation was developed by Senate Finance Committee
Chairman Mike Crapo and Ranking Member Ron Wyden.
"This bipartisan legislation answers years of frustration felt by Americans
trying to do their best to follow our tax laws," Crapo said in September.
Wyden focused more directly on the financial impact of delays and poor service.
"Millions of Americans are struggling with the rising cost of living, and the
last thing they need is to be hit by tax scammers who are able to dodge IRS
scrutiny," said Wyden. "Our bipartisan legislation makes it easier for Americans
to get filing assistance and ensures refunds get out the door and into
Americans' hands on time."
The bill wouldn't change individual income tax rates. Instead, it focuses on
making the existing tax system work better for the people using it.

 Your tax refund could arrive faster
One of the biggest potential benefits involves refunds, with the bill requiring
the IRS to expand electronic processing of paper returns. Paper returns
generally take longer to process, particularly when the IRS faces backlogs, so
digitizing more of them could help refunds reach taxpayers sooner.
The bill would also improve the IRS's "Where's My Refund?" tools, giving
taxpayers clearer information about when their money might arrive and what steps
to take if something goes wrong.
That could be particularly useful if you're counting on a refund to pay down
debt, cover household expenses, or rebuild your emergency savings. However, the
legislation wouldn't guarantee that every taxpayer receives a refund by a
particular date.
 Getting through to the IRS can be difficult
The bill would expand callback options so taxpayers could request a return call
from more IRS phone numbers rather than remaining on hold. It would also improve
online accounts, allowing taxpayers and their authorized representatives to
access more tax information and communicate with the agency electronically.
In practice, those changes could make it easier to review correspondence,
respond to notices, and resolve questions without relying entirely on phone
calls or mailed documents. If you've ever received an IRS letter and struggled
to understand what to do next, those changes could make a meaningful difference.

 The bill could protect you from costly IRS delays
Taxpayers could face penalties when returns or payments aren't submitted on time,
even when technical problems complicate the process. The legislation includes a
provision designed to provide clearer protection for electronic submissions.
Under the proposal, qualifying electronic returns and payments submitted by the
deadline would generally receive the same timely-filing protection as mailed
documents. As a result, taxpayers could have stronger protection from penalties
when an electronic submission is sent on time but isn't immediately processed.
The bill would also strengthen taxpayer rights in disputes with the IRS,
including expanding certain opportunities to challenge agency decisions. Those
protections could matter if you're facing penalties, contesting a tax
assessment, or trying to resolve an error that affects your finances.
 Tax fraud victims could receive stronger protections
The bill would also reinforce protections for taxpayers caught up in fraud or
identity theft. Identity theft involving tax returns could create serious
problems, including delayed refunds and additional IRS scrutiny.
The bill includes measures intended to prevent fraud victims from remaining
under indefinite examination because of someone else's actions. It would also
strengthen oversight of paid tax preparers, who aren't all subject to the same
minimum competency requirements.
The proposed changes could help protect taxpayers from dishonest or unqualified
preparers whose mistakes or misconduct may lead to penalties, delayed refunds,
or audits. That matters because even when someone else prepares your return,
you're generally responsible for ensuring the information submitted to the IRS
is accurate.
 What would change for your next tax return?
The legislation could eventually make filing taxes and resolving IRS problems
easier, but it hasn't become law. Although the Senate approved the bill, the
House still needs to agree to the Senate's changes before the bill is sent
to the president for his signature.
Even if enacted, some improvements would require the IRS to update its systems
and procedures before taxpayers notice a difference. Until then, you could still
use existing IRS tools to check your refund status, review your tax records, and
manage notices through your online account.

 Bottom line
Republicans and Democrats have united behind legislation that could improve how
the IRS handles refunds, taxpayer questions, tax disputes, and fraud. The Senate
has approved the bill, but the proposed changes won't take effect unless the
legislation becomes law.
The Taxpayer Assistance and Service Act wouldn't lower your income tax rate or
automatically increase your refund. However, it could make getting a refund,
resolving mistakes, and dealing with the IRS faster and less stressful,
particularly for Americans trying to cope with increasing
bills .
